# Intro

## Intro

- Last lecture gave us traded factors: market, SMB, HML, and momentum [@FamaFrench1993; @Carhart1997]
- Today: what do those factors actually represent?
- Risk exposures?
- Or firm characteristics dressed up as factors?

## Flight Plan

- Part I: set up the characteristics-versus-covariances fight
- Part II: the Daniel-Titman challenge and the rebuttal [@DanielTitman1997; @DavisFamaFrench2000]
- Part III: why empirical design can flip the answer [@ChordiaGoyalShanken2017; @LewellenNagelShanken2010]
- Part IV: a modern reconciliation [@KellyPruittSu2019]

# Part I: What Is Being Priced?

## Last Lecture Left a Gap

- @FamaFrench1993 showed that SMB and HML help price test portfolios
- But pricing success does not pin down economic interpretation
- A factor can work in the data for more than one reason

## Two Stories

- Story 1: expected returns are driven by factor loadings
- Story 2: expected returns are driven by characteristics directly
- In the data, these two objects move together a lot

## A Clean Risk-Based Prediction

$$
R_{i,t}-R_{f,t}=\alpha_i+\beta_i^\top f_t+\varepsilon_{i,t}
$$

- If risk loadings are primitive, higher $\beta_i$ should mean higher average returns
- Once we hold characteristics fixed, beta differences should still matter
- That is the Daniel-Titman test

## Why Separation Is Hard

- High book-to-market firms often have different factor exposures
- Small firms often have different factor exposures
- Portfolio sorts change characteristics and covariances at the same time
- The empirical fight is really about identification

# Part II: The Debate

## Daniel-Titman: Question and Design

- Core question: do returns follow characteristics or factor loadings? [@DanielTitman1997]
- Hold size and book-to-market roughly fixed
- Then compare portfolios with different loadings on the Fama-French factors

## Characteristic-Matched Portfolios

- Sort stocks on characteristics first
- Inside those buckets, form portfolios with different factor exposures
- This tries to break the usual link between characteristics and betas
- If FF risk is the whole story, return spreads should track loadings

## Placeholder: Daniel-Titman Design

- Add schematic: same size / BE-ME, different factor loadings

\vfill

## Daniel-Titman: Main Finding

- Return differences line up more with characteristics than with loadings [@DanielTitman1997]
- High book-to-market still earns more, even when factor exposures are similar
- That is a direct hit to the risk-based reading of SMB and HML

## What Exactly Was Challenged?

- Not that factors forecast returns
- The challenged claim is deeper: are SMB and HML truly priced risks?
- Maybe factor models work because they proxy for characteristics

## Davis-Fama-French: The Reply

- @DavisFamaFrench2000 push back on the characteristic story
- Their point: the value premium is robust over a longer sample
- They argue that covariance differences remain inside characteristic sorts
- The same evidence can still be consistent with factor pricing

## Why the Rebuttal Matters

- Characteristics and covariances are empirically entangled
- If sorts do not isolate one from the other, interpretation stays open
- The debate is not settled by one successful portfolio experiment

## Placeholder: Value Premium Comparison

- Add table or figure: characteristics story vs covariance story

\vfill

## Chordia-Goyal-Shanken: Individual Stocks

- Move from sorted portfolios to individual stocks [@ChordiaGoyalShanken2017]
- Correct for errors-in-variables in estimated betas
- Betas regain explanatory power once the design changes
- Conclusion: the answer depends on the empirical protocol

## What Changes When You Leave Portfolios?

- Portfolios reduce noise, but they also engineer factor structure
- Individual-stock tests are noisier, but closer to the raw cross-section
- This tradeoff becomes central for the whole literature

# Part III: Why Tests Break

## Lewellen-Nagel-Shanken: The Deeper Problem

- Many factor models appear to price the usual test assets [@LewellenNagelShanken2010]
- Small alphas and high cross-sectional $R^2$ can be misleading
- False models can still look successful

## Why Many False Models Look Good

- Test portfolios are highly correlated with each other
- Average returns live in a low-dimensional space
- Many different factor sets can span that space approximately
- Good fit is weaker evidence than it looks

## The Cross-Sectional Regression

$$
\bar R_i = \hat \lambda^\top \hat \beta_i + \hat \alpha_i
$$

- This second pass is fragile when $\hat \beta_i$ is noisy
- It is also fragile when test assets are constructed from the same characteristics
- The problem is power, not only specification

## What This Means for the Literature

- Apparent pricing success does not uniquely identify the right factors
- Empirical asset pricing can easily overproduce "good" models
- This is one reason the factor zoo arrives later

## Bridge to the Next Lecture

- Weak identification plus many candidate predictors is a dangerous combination
- Once researchers search widely, successful factors proliferate
- Next lecture: why the zoo got so large [@HarveyLiuZhu2016; @McLeanPontiff2016]

# Part IV: Characteristics Are Covariances

## Kelly-Pruitt-Su: The Main Idea

- @KellyPruittSu2019 do not treat characteristics and covariances as rivals
- Characteristics forecast returns because they forecast latent factor loadings
- The debate becomes: how are betas measured?

## A Unified Representation

$$
\mathbb{E}_t[R_{i,t+1}] = \beta_{i,t}^\top \lambda_t,
\qquad
\beta_{i,t} = b(z_{i,t})
$$

- $z_{i,t}$ denotes firm characteristics
- Characteristics enter by shaping time-varying exposures
- They look "direct" only because the true factors are latent

## Characteristics as Beta Proxies

- Daniel-Titman were right that characteristics predict returns
- Risk-based models were right that covariances matter
- Both can be true when characteristics proxy for loadings on latent factors

## Taking Stock

- Daniel-Titman challenged the risk interpretation
- Davis-Fama-French and Chordia-Goyal-Shanken showed the answer depends on design
- Lewellen-Nagel-Shanken explained why many models seem to work
- Kelly-Pruitt-Su reconcile the debate
